title: How Google got its name
hook: Google began life as BackRub, and its name is a misspelt giant number.
peek: Before it was Google, the Stanford search project of Larry Page and Sergey Brin was called BackRub. Its new name came from googol, a 1 followed by 100 zeros, spelt the wrong way when someone checked a web address.
lede: In 1996 two Stanford graduate students, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, built a search engine that ranked pages by the links pointing to them. They called it BackRub, after those backlinks. When it needed a grander name, they reached for a number: the googol, a 1 followed by 100 zeros. The spelling they ended up with was a happy accident.

bullets.text: BackRub ran on Stanford's own network and judged a page by how many other pages linked to it, and how important those were. That idea, later called PageRank, became the heart of Google.

The usual account is that a fellow student, Sean Anderson, typed google.com instead of googol.com while checking whether the name was free. Page liked it, and the google.com domain was registered in September 1997.

The word googol was coined around 1920 by Milton Sirotta, the nine-year-old nephew of the mathematician Edward Kasner. Kasner wanted a fun name for a huge number, and he made it famous in a 1940 book.

The joke carried on. Google's headquarters in Mountain View is the Googleplex, a nod to the googolplex, which is 1 followed by a googol zeros, far too many to write out even with every atom in the universe.
